Title: A Convex Feasibility Problem for Which Douglas-Rachford Converges Only Weakly
Authors: Jan Quan, Panagiotis Patrinos
Date: Tue Oct 20 15:51:26 2026

We provide two closed, convex sets with nonempty intersection and an initial point for which the Douglas-Rachford algorithm converges weakly but not strongly. This resolves an open question as noted earlier by Aragón Artacho, Borwein and Tam (2014, Remark 2.2). Our construction is a simple lift of a recent construction by Bauschke and Tung concerning firmly nonexpansive operators.--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

  * # The optimality of silver step sizes for gradient descent

Oct 02, 2026 24 min read

  * math-OC

> Overview
> 
> Gradient descent can converge faster than the familiar O(1/n) rate without adding momentum: a carefully arranged sequence of long and short steps achieves the silver exponent p sil​=lo g 2​(1+2​)≈1.2716. Yuhan Ye and Kaizhao Liu prove that this exponent is optimal among predetermined nonnegative step-size schedules, up to a subpolynomial factor. They also identify the smaller optimal exponent for a single schedule that must work at every stopping horizon (Ye & Liu, 2026).
> 
> The proof constructs smooth convex functions whose gradients rotate before selected long steps. These steps pass the trajectory from one coordinate pair to the next. A recursive optimization over the selected steps reduces the lower bound to a scalar inequality containing the silver ratio. This post develops the prerequisites and the central calculations, including the correction term needed to make the recursion work and the record-time argument for the anytime result.

The primary source is Silver Rate Is (Almost) Optimal for Gradient Descent, arXiv:2609.09152v2, revised September 10, 2026. Statements and lemma numbers below refer to that version. The illustrations are original TikZ drawings; the local iterate drawing is schematic, while the gradient arc and scalar curves use the displayed formulas.

## 🏷️ Preliminaries: Smooth Convex Optimization

### Convexity, smoothness, and the optimization model

We minimize a differentiable function f:R d→R with at least one minimizer x∗​. Throughout, ⟨⋅,⋅⟩ and ∥⋅∥ denote the Euclidean inner product and norm.

Convexity is equivalent to the supporting-plane inequality

f(y)≥f(x)+⟨∇f(x),y−x⟩.

The function is L-smooth if its gradient is L-Lipschitz:

∥∇f(x)−∇f(y)∥≤L∥x−y∥.

Integrating the gradient along the segment from x to y gives the corresponding upper bound

f(y)≤f(x)+⟨∇f(x),y−x⟩+2 L​∥y−x∥2.

These hypotheses do not require strong convexity, a unique minimizer, or a positive lower bound on curvature. 
f(x−h∇f(x))≤f(x)−h(1−2 h​)∥∇f(x)∥2.

When h>2, this inequality no longer guarantees descent. Yet occasional long steps can improve the error after a whole block of iterations. An analysis that demands progress at every individual step cannot capture this mechanism.

### The silver schedule

Let

ρ:=1+2​,p sil​:=lo g 2​ρ.

For an integer t≥1, let v 2​(t) be the largest integer j≥0 for which 2 j divides t. The silver schedule is

h t​=1+ρ v 2​(t)−1.

Its first seven steps are

2​, 2, 2​, 1+ρ, 2​, 2, 2​.

Write S(k) for its first 2 k−1 entries. Then

S(k+1)=(S(k), 1+ρ k−1, S(k)),S(1)=(2​).

Altschuler and Parrilo prove an O(n−p sil​) function-value guarantee at completed horizons n=2 k−1 (Altschuler & Parrilo, 2025). For any prescribed finite horizon, one can use the largest completed block that fits and append zero steps; its length is a constant fraction of the horizon, preserving the exponent. Although the silver formula defines an infinite sequence, this guarantee at completed blocks does not provide the same rate at every prefix.

### Finite-horizon and anytime guarantees

In the finite-horizon, or non-anytime, problem, a different schedule may be chosen for each n. Its minimax error is

r n∗​:=H∈[0,∞)n in f​R n​(H).

In the anytime problem, one infinite schedule h=(h t​)t≥1​ must work for every horizon. At horizon n, its error is evaluated using the prefix H n​=(h 1​,…,h n​). A guarantee must therefore survive interruption during a block, including immediately after a long step.

This distinction concerns compatibility between schedules at different horizons. The objective class and the update rule are the same in both problems.

## 🏷️ Main Results and Their Quantifiers

Set

p any​:=1+p sil​2 p sil​​≈1.1195,δ n​:=lo g n lo g lo g n​​.

> Finite-horizon lower bound: Theorem 1.1
> 
> There is an absolute constant C>0 such that, for every sufficiently large n and every predetermined nonnegative schedule H∈[0,∞)n,
> 
> R n​(H)≥n−(p sil​+C δ n​).

> Anytime lower bound: Theorem 1.2
> 
> There is an absolute constant C>0 such that every infinite predetermined nonnegative schedule has infinitely many horizons n satisfying
> 
> R n​(H n​)≥n−(p any​+C δ n​).

The first theorem holds for every schedule at each sufficiently large horizon. The second holds along infinitely many horizons for each infinite schedule; it does not assert the displayed bound at every horizon. At different horizons the supremum defining R n​ may use different objectives.

The factor concealed in the changing exponent is

n−C δ n​=exp(−C lo g n lo g lo g n​).

It tends to zero, but more slowly than any fixed negative power of n. The result therefore rules out every fixed polynomial improvement over the silver exponent. It does not establish a constant-factor lower bound Ω(n−p sil​), nor rule out all improvements by logarithmic factors.

Together with the silver upper bound and the anytime construction of Zhang, Lee, Du, and Chen (Zhang et al., 2025), the results determine these optimal polynomial exponents:

Method or schedule requirement  | Achievable exponent  | Lower-bound conclusion
--- | --- | ---
Constant-step gradient descent  | 1  | A baseline achievable rate
Predetermined nonnegative GD, prescribed horizon  | p sil​≈1.2716  | No fixed larger exponent uniformly over objectives
One predetermined nonnegative GD schedule, all horizons  | p any​≈1.1195  | No fixed larger exponent at every sufficiently large horizon
General accelerated first-order methods  | 2  | A broader algorithm class, allowing auxiliary iterates

> Scope of the theorem
> 
> The lower bounds concern the final iterate of ordinary GD with predetermined nonnegative step sizes on general smooth convex objectives. It is convex, 1-smooth, flat to the left, and affine sufficiently far to the right. In the affine region, the gradient is constant, making the final loss easy to compute exactly.

## 🏷️ Checkpoints and the Geometric Bottleneck

Fix any schedule h=(h 1​,…,h n​). Select indices

T={t 1​<⋯<t k​},t 0​=0,t k+1​=n+1,

and define

b i​=h t i​​,s i​=t=t i−1​+1∑t i​−1​h t​.

The b i​ are checkpoints, typically long steps. The s i​ are sums of the intervening steps, not counts of iterations. In particular, s k+1​ is the sum after the final checkpoint.

Earlier constructions join one-sided Huber terms on adjacent coordinates. While a term involving x(i)−x(i+1) is affine, its gradient is proportional to e i​−e i+1​. A GD step decreases coordinate i and increases coordinate i+1 by equal amounts. Both changes shrink the difference keeping that term active. This double consumption of the active coordinate gap leads to a transfer ratio

2(2+s i​)b i​​

and, for positive step-size schedules, the checkpoint lower bound

R n​(h)≥4(1+s k+1​)1​i=1∏k​[2(2+s i​)b i​​]2.

This is Fact 2.1 of the paper, attributed to Jung, Cho, and Yun (Jung, Cho & Yun, 2026). Its recursive analysis gives the exponent lo g 2​(1+3​)≈1.4500. For a lower bound, a smaller exponent is stronger: n−1.2716 is larger than n−1.4500 at large n.

Ye and Liu reduce the coefficient of s i​ toward 1. During much of an intervening block, the gradient points horizontally, consuming the current coordinate with little increase in the next. Near the selected step, it turns almost vertically, allowing that step to raise the next coordinate substantially.

The necessary turn must still be compatible with convexity and smoothness, and the previous component must stay inactive after the next one begins. Both requirements are built into the local objective.
The paper supplies the following calculus argument.

> Proof of the silver inequality
> 
> Let p=p sil​, α=p−1∈(0,1/3), and F(z)=z p+(1−z)p+[z(1−z)]p. For 0<z<1/2,
> 
> p[z(1−z)]α F′(z)​=ϕ(z):=(1−z)−α−z−α+1−2 z.
> 
> Differentiating twice gives
> 
> ϕ′′(z)=α(α+1)[(1−z)−α−2−z−α−2]<0.
> 
> Thus ϕ′ decreases strictly. Its endpoint behavior is ϕ′(0+)=+∞ and
> 
> ϕ′(1/2)=α 2 α+2−2<0.
> 
> The last inequality follows from α<1/3. Consequently, ϕ first increases and then decreases. Since ϕ(0+)=−∞, ϕ(1/2)=0, and ϕ′(1/2)<0, it is positive just left of 1/2 and crosses zero exactly once in the interior. Therefore F first decreases and then increases on [0,1/2].
> 
> Its maximum on this half-interval is at an endpoint. Those values are
> 
> F(0)=1,F(1/2)=ρ 2​+ρ 2 1​=1.
> 
> Symmetry gives the other half. Equality occurs at z=0,1/2,1.

### Perturbing the geometry

The actual construction needs ϵ,γ>0, hence c>1. With

τ=ϵ 1/p,ν=1/p,

the normalized scalar constraint becomes

u+v+(c−ϵ)uv≥1,

and the target, including the correction term, is

u 1/p+v 1/p−τ(uv)1/p≥1.

Lemma 3.5 quantifies how much to increase p to retain this inequality. For p∈[p sil​,3/2], 0<c−ϵ≤2, and τ≤1/10, it suffices that

p−p sil​≥(c−ϵ−1)+​+6 ϵ 1/p,t+​:=max{t,0}.

The useful slack estimate is

z p+(1−z)p+(c−ϵ)[z(1−z)]p≤1−[p−p sil​−(c−ϵ−1)+​]z(1−z).

To obtain it, differentiate with respect to p. The inequalities −lo g z≥1−z and −lo g(1−z)≥z give a decrease of at least z(1−z) per unit increase in p. The deviation of c−ϵ from 1 costs at most (c−ϵ−1)+​z(1−z). Finally, the perturbed boundary Y=(1−X)/(1−τ X) differs from 1−X by at most τ X(1−X)/(1−τ); a mean-value estimate costs at most 6 τ X(1−X). The displayed condition pays for both errors.

This quantitative slack is necessary near z=0,1, where a merely uniform continuity argument would not control the vanishing gap.

THE DOUGLAS–RACHFORD ALGORITHM CONVERGES ONLY WEAKLY*

MINH N. BÙI† AND PATRICK L. COMBETTES‡

**Abstract.** We show that the weak convergence of the Douglas–Rachford algorithm for finding a zero of the sum of two maximally monotone operators cannot be improved to strong convergence. Likewise, we show that strong convergence can fail for the method of partial inverses.

**Key words.** Douglas–Rachford algorithm, method of partial inverses, monotone operator, operator splitting, strong convergence.

The original Douglas–Rachford splitting algorithm was designed to decompose positive systems of linear equations [3]. It evolved in [5] into a powerful method for finding a zero of the sum of two maximally monotone operators in Hilbert spaces, a problem which is ubiquitous in applied mathematics (see [1] for background on monotone operators). In this context, the Douglas–Rachford algorithm constitutes a prime decomposition method in areas such as control, partial differential equations, optimization, statistics, variational inequalities, mechanics, optimal transportation, machine learning, and signal processing. --------------------------------------------------------------------------------
